newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Store sales, housing, 2-yr notes.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Store sales, housing, 2-yr notes.

text.p: Fresh data on U.S. housing starts, chain and department store sales and the monthly two-year Treasury note auction will highlight U.S. government securities trading on Tuesday.

Early in the trading session (at 0830 EST/1330 GMT), the government will release October housing starts figures. Economists expect these to rise slightly to an annualized rate of 1.443 million after September's very sharp drop to an annualized rate of 1.438 million.

"Housing is the most interest-rate sensitive sector," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "If the economy is really slowing in response to higher interest rates, this is one of the places where we should see that."

One half hour after the government's housing report, the BTM/Schroder weekly report on U.S. chain and department store sales is due. Those data, along with the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Redbook store sales figures that are released nearly six hours later, are acquiring a new prominence in the market's eyes.
That's because economists say the pivotal issue for the markets now is whether consumers will spend enough during the holiday season to boost fourth-quarter economic activity.
"With each passing week, the closer we get to Christmas, the more closely we have to watch these weekly indicators," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities.

The BTM/Schroders index rose 0.4 percent in the week ended November 10. "The key for the market now is fourth-quarter (consumer) spending," said Dimick. "Another 0.4 percent read on the Mitsubishi index would certainly get attention."

The juxtaposition of the housing data at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, and the Treasury's monthly auction of $18.25 billion in two-year notes four-and-a-half hours later could cap any rally that might ensue if housing data were unexpectedly weak.
Normally, weak housing data would be friendly for the bond market. But dealers also have to be concerned that yields on the two-year notes are not so low that buyers will walk away from the auction.
"A lot of people are wondering who wants to buy two-year notes trading only 40 basis points above the Fed funds rate," said Dimick.
"They think this spread has compressed nearly as much as it can without the presumption of a dramatic slowdown or Fed easing being priced into the market," he said.

If that presumption did take hold, two-year note yields would trade through the Federal funds rate (of 5-1/4 percent), said Dimick. "But someone who does not believe the economy is racing up to the brink of recession or that the Fed will be cutting rates in the first quarter might be nervous buying two-year notes near 5-5/8 percent," he said. In when-issued trade late Monday, the two-year notes to be sold on Tuesday were yielding 5.6725 percent.
The five-year notes to be sold on Wednesday were yielding 5.97 percent.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond was down 3/32 to 100-13/32 in late trade, yielding 6.47 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-3/16 percent and 5-1/4 percent.
